findings.title: Cache key uses Python's unstable hash(), breaking caching and invalidation across processes
findings.body: The cache key is built with `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's built-in `hash()` for tuples/strings is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED randomization), so different gunicorn/uwsgi workers — and the same worker after a restart — produce different keys for the identical project set. Consequences: (1) the 60-second cache is almost never shared between workers, so the claimed performance optimization does not work; (2) worse, `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 67) computes the key the same way, so a process handling an allowlist change will delete a key that no other process ever reads, making invalidation silently useless. Additionally, `hash()` collisions across different project-id sets can cause one organization's cached eligibility to be applied to a different set of projects, which is a data-integrity risk (wrong counts served). Use a deterministic key, e.g. `':'.join(map(str, sorted(project_ids)))` or an md5/sha digest.

findings.title: Substring match on 'event.type:error' mis-classifies negated or quoted queries as error-focused
findings.body: `_is_error_focused_query` does `if "event.type:error" in query` on the raw lowercased query string. This returns True for queries like `!event.type:error` (explicitly excluding errors) or `message:"event.type:error"` (the string inside a quoted value). In those cases the discover query is not restricted to error events, yet `count()` will be rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)`, producing wrong (under)counts for transactions/other event types. The check should parse the query with the search grammar (or at minimum check that the token isn't negated/quoted) rather than doing a naive substring test.

findings.title: Upsampling eligibility uses the outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`
findings.body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` closes over the endpoint-level `dataset`, but the query actually runs against `scoped_dataset`. In the dashboard-widget split path (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is invoked with `discover` and a synthesized query like `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction`, or with `scoped_dataset` for transaction-like widgets, while eligibility is still decided from the original request dataset. This means a widget originally on the errors dataset that is rerouted to a transaction/discover query can still get `count()` rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (wrong counts for non-error events), and conversely an errors-only discover subquery can fail the `_is_error_focused_query` check because the raw request query lacks `event.type:error`, so no upsampling is applied where it should be. The scoped dataset (and the effective query string) should be passed to the eligibility check.

findings.title: upsampled_count registered as a public function without private=True
findings.body: The new `SnQLFunction("upsampled_count", ...)` is added to the discover function converter without `private=True`, unlike the neighboring internal-only functions in the same mapping which are marked `private=True`. This exposes `upsampled_count()` as a user-queryable aggregate in the public Discover query API: any user can append it to a query and get `sum(sample_weight)` on arbitrary data where `sample_weight` is null or meaningless, returning misleading numbers. Since this function is only meant to be injected server-side by the error-upsampling path, it should be marked `private=True`.

findings.title: Accidentally committed git submodule pointing at the base commit
findings.body: The PR adds a `sentry-repo` gitlink (subproject commit a5d290951..., which is exactly the PR's base commit). This looks like a local clone of the repo that was accidentally `git add`ed. It will create a broken submodule entry (no `.gitmodules` URL) in the tree and should be removed from the PR.
